overview: This file traces silk as a strategic commodity in U.S.–Japanese relations from 1940 to 1944. It begins with American investigations into shortages of Chinese silk waste, Japanese control of supplies, and suspected diversions to Japan or Germany; follows a Japanese-backed proposal to barter government-owned raw silk for American petroleum and other goods amid tightening U.S. economic pressure; and documents disputes over Japanese export quotas, the financing of the American raw-silk trade, and the exclusion of an American firm from Japan’s exporters’ association. Later records revisit attorney Raoul E. Desvernine’s unauthorized barter activities through Department of Justice and possible Logan Act inquiries, while wartime reports describe declining cocoon and silk production in Japan and the contraction and Japanese control of the industry in occupied China.
interest: Shows silk trade entangled with defense procurement, economic warfare and sanctions circumvention before and during the Pacific War.
